title: A companion text
hookLine: the book you'll keep reading for years: Augustine heard a child chant "take up and read", and the same book spoke next to his friend
tomorrow: how long did Ezra keep reading, and how much each day?

lines: UNDER A FIG TREE IN MILAN.
cards: A song comes through a neighbor's wall, half heard, and won't leave your head. Augustine heard something like that, in a garden in Milan.
He was under a fig tree, crying, stuck between the life he had and the one he wanted.
Then, from a house next door, a child's voice, boy or girl, he couldn't tell, chanting the same words over and over: "Take up and read; Take up and read."

teach.h: THE FIRST LINES HIS EYES FELL ON.
teach.b: He'd left a book where his friend was sitting, the letters of the apostle Paul. He went back, picked it up, opened it, and read in silence the first lines his eyes fell on.

teach.h: PUT YE ON THE LORD JESUS CHRIST.
teach.b: One of them: "But put ye on the Lord Jesus Christ." He didn't read further. He didn't need to.
In his Confessions he says the darkness of doubt was gone.

He marked the place, closed the book, and told his friend Alypius, who was with him. Then Alypius asked to see it, and read on, past where Augustine stopped. The next line was about receiving someone weak in the faith.
Alypius took that one as his own. Same book, same page, a different word for a different friend.

teach.h: THE WORD OF GOD IS QUICK.
teach.b: Christians teach that scripture is living: "the word of God is quick, and powerful," as Hebrews puts it, quick meaning alive.
That's one reason Christians return to the same book for a lifetime and expect it to speak again. A companion text, on your own path, is one book like that. Not the newest.
The one you can hold in your hands for years, and still find a line waiting.

how: Christians read the Bible as a living word and return to it for a lifetime. People on many paths keep one companion text, read slowly and often, for years.

games.q: a friend has read a dozen spiritual books this year and remembers none. by Augustine's garden, what might help?
o: choose one book to keep returning to, expecting it to speak again.
read faster, so the right line turns up sooner.
stop reading and wait for a voice to say which book.
games.why: Augustine's moment came from one book; Christians read scripture as living, a book that speaks again and again.

practice: Set the book you'd most like to keep reading in front of you, or any book you love. Look at the cover, the worn corners, the creases in the spine.
Open it anywhere, let your eyes fall on one line, the way Augustine's did, and stop there.
